title: What To Do If Attacked By A Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Citing APA data that 44 percent of teachers report being physically attacked by a student, Linsin lays out concrete personal-safety guidance for a worst-case scenario. He first describes ordinary preventive habits — constant awareness of student location, keeping physical distance as a default posture, positioning oneself near a wall, and avoiding kneeling down close to students — that reduce the odds of ever being caught off guard. He then details two safe positions if an attack does occur: escaping beyond striking distance entirely, which he calls the best option, or, if escape is impossible, closing the distance and bear-hugging the attacker to minimize the danger of the one-to-six-foot striking zone, describing the specific mechanics of the hold. He explicitly discourages fighting back offensively except as an absolute last resort given the physical and professional risks, and he treats the topic candidly as an unpleasant but necessary subject for teachers to have thought through in advance.
points: 44 percent of teachers report being physically attacked by a student, according to APA data cited in the article, and violence is described as rising post-pandemic.
Ordinary preventive habits — constant supervision, default distance from students, positioning near a wall — reduce the odds of ever being caught unprepared.
If attacked, the safest options are either escaping entirely beyond striking distance or, if escape is impossible, closing the distance to bear-hug the attacker.
The one-to-six-foot 'danger zone' around an attacker is where the greatest physical damage occurs and should be avoided or moved through quickly.
Fighting back offensively is discouraged except as an absolute last resort, given the physical, legal, and professional risks involved.
quotes: According to the American Psychological Association, 44 percent of teachers report being physically attacked by a student.
If attacked by a student, there are two places you must be to stay safe. Only two. The first is beyond striking distance. Meaning, out of range of your attacker.
Within the one to six foot zone that is the attacker’s striking distance. It is here that you will suffer the greatest amount of injury and physical damage.
So what happens if a student closes on you and into your danger zone while throwing violent punches and/or kicks? So fast that you can’t get away? You close on them.
As soon as you make contact, wrap your arms around them, grip one hand around your opposite wrist (in a monkey grip), place your ear tight to their chest, and hang on tight.
Either they will be injured or you will. It will also encourage other students to jump in. You’ll lose your job and need a good lawyer.
